metadata.title: What Comes First When You Hire Abroad?
metadata.purpose: Answer what a legal/HR team must decide before drafting an employment contract for a first hire in a new country: how the role is classified and who the legal employer will be, not the contract itself. Lands the carry-out that the contract can't fix a bad classification -- the country's labor law decides who counts as an employee, not the page.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible international-hiring account from the title/family rather than lifting facts that were never written.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the Berlin developer: full control over hours, one client, your equipment -- employee-shaped regardless of the contract's label)

beats.narration_text: A legal team gets asked to hire someone in Germany, and the reflex is to draft a contract. Here's why the reflex misfires: the contract is not the thing that decides who this person legally is. The classification does — and the classification is set before you write a word. I'm Liam, in for Bear. Let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. The word on the page — 'contractor' — is an input the labor law tests against reality; it is not the verdict. The law is designed that way for a reason: if the label decided the classification, every employer would relabel their way out of paying benefits. So the test looks at mechanism, not language. Set the hours, hand over your laptop, take them as their only client — a local court reads that as an employment relationship and re-labels the page for you. The contract lost that argument the moment the work started.

shot.new_visual_element: A contract card with an editable 'CONTRACTOR' label; behind it, clock/toolbox/single-client icons all light up employee-shaped anyway; a stamp comes down over the label reading EMPLOYEE

production_viz.label: The label doesn't decide the classification
production_viz.mechanic: A card headed 'CONTRACT' with a text field reading 'CONTRACTOR' in its header. Three status icons beneath it -- a clock, a toolbox, a single-client badge -- fade in and light up one at a time, all employee-shaped, while the header label stays unchanged. A stamp shape comes down over the header anyway, marking 'EMPLOYEE' in accent color. A caption fades in beneath: 'the page doesn't decide this.'

beats.narration_text: Here's the actual machinery a real hiring plan runs before anyone drafts a contract — three checks, in this order. One: how the role is classified. Two: who's the legal employer on paper — your own entity in that country, or an Employer of Record standing in for one. Three: which local rules override anything you write — notice periods, statutory benefits, termination protections. Now watch the anchor. Berlin. Developer. Forty hours a week, one client, working on your laptop with your tools. Hold that in mind — we're coming back to it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three check chips lighting in turn (classification / legal employer / mandatory terms), then a dim, icon-only developer card set off to the side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three checks, then the unclassified hire
production_viz.mechanic: Three chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a check (CLASSIFICATION / LEGAL EMPLOYER / MANDATORY TERMS), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'developer -- Berlin' with icon-only marks (clock, laptop, single-client badge) and no fields filled in -- visibly incomplete against the three-check shape just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Run the Berlin developer through the checks. Full control of their hours, one client, your equipment — every dimension the labor law tests reads as employee. That's what the machinery decides, and no page rewrite fixes it. Two consequences fall out. First: passing as contractor-shaped today does not lock in — change how the work actually runs and the classification can flip later, same contract, no signature required. Second: landing on employee does not mean spinning up a German entity by Friday. An Employer of Record can be the legal employer on paper while you build your own. They optimized that for speed — you get a legal home without owning one — at the cost of a middle layer taking a per-head cut every month.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim developer card lighting up with all three checks filled and moving into the main list; then split into 'classification can still flip' and 'doesn't require your own entity'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- classified, not locked in
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in one field at a time (classification: employee-shaped / legal employer: entity or EOR / mandatory terms: notice + benefits) until fully lit, then slides into a row alongside other completed entries. It splits into two cards: left reads 'contractor-shaped today' with a struck-through 'LOCKED IN' beneath it labelled 'classification can still flip'; right reads 'employee-shaped' with a faint 'Employer of Record available' card at its edge labelled 'doesn't require your own entity'.

beats.narration_text: The contract can't fix a bad classification — that's the whole thing. The labor law decides who this person legally is; the page just records the decision. Work out the classification and the legal employer before you draft a word. This works if you value getting the shape right up front; it fails hard if you value moving fast on a template.

props.quote: The contract can't fix a bad classification. Work out how the role is classified and who the legal employer will be before you draft anything -- the country's labor law decides that, not the label on the page.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Replace COUNTRY with the one you're actually hiring in — the answers get much sharper. It walks a frontier model through the same three checks in order: classification, legal employer, mandatory terms. What comes back is a country-specific version of the machinery we just took apart. Go deeper: ask the same model what changes about all three answers if the person moves countries mid-employment — that's where the classification runs into remote-work reality, and the trade-offs get interesting.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm planning to hire our first employee in [COUNTRY]. Before I draft a contract, walk me through three things in order: (1) CLASSIFICATION — under [COUNTRY]'s labor law, how would this role most likely be classified as employee vs contractor, based on control of hours, provision of equipment, and number of clients? Name the specific tests courts apply there. (2) LEGAL EMPLOYER — compare opening our own local entity vs using an Employer of Record on setup cost, timeline, tax and payroll obligations, and termination risk. (3) MANDATORY TERMS — once the person is classified as an employee, which statutory terms override anything I put in the contract (notice period, severance, benefits, working-time limits, termination protections). Answer each section with rules specific to [COUNTRY], and flag anything a US-shaped employment contract would get wrong.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what changes about all three answers if the person moves countries mid-employment — for example, works remotely from a different EU state for a quarter?
